# secaudit-passive

The Codex form of SecAudit's `/secaudit-passive` command. It runs when the user names it (`$secaudit-passive`), and
whatever they wrote after the name is its arguments.

## Reading this under Codex

The kit's skills and its verifier agent are written once, in Claude Code's vocabulary, and this
plugin carries them unchanged. Read them with this table:

| The text says | Under Codex |
| --- | --- |
| the **security-audit** skill | this plugin's `security-audit` skill (`secaudit:security-audit`). Open its `SKILL.md` and follow it, `references/` included. |
| `/secaudit`, any `/command` | the skill of the same name: `$secaudit`, `$secaudit-code`, `$secaudit-deps`, `$secaudit-passive`. |
| Read / Grep / Glob | shell read commands (`cat`, `sed -n`, `rg`, `ls`) |
| WebSearch / WebFetch | the web search tool |
| Task, "a background subagent" | spawn an agent and wait for its result |
| the `secaudit-verifier` agent | the custom agent of that name when this session has one; otherwise a default agent given the `developer_instructions` of [agents/secaudit-verifier.toml](../../agents/secaudit-verifier.toml) as its instructions. Either way it is read-only: it reports, it does not edit. |

Two things differ from Claude Code, and both matter:

1. **The command allowlist is a rule here, not a harness limit.** In Claude Code this command may
   run only the shell commands below without asking. Codex has no per-skill allowlist, so the
   same list binds as a rule: while this skill is running, ask the user before running anything
   outside it.

   `curl -sS`, `curl -I`, `command -v`, `dig`, `nslookup`, `testssl.sh`, `sslscan`

2. **The authorization hook runs only once it is trusted.** Codex skips a plugin's hook until the
   user has reviewed it in `/hooks`. Until then the passive-by-default posture rests on the
   skill's own authorization gate, which binds either way. A command that was not blocked is not
   a command that was authorized.

## Procedure

Run the **security-audit** skill in **passive-only mode** against: the arguments given with this skill — whatever the user wrote after `$secaudit-passive`

Only low-impact, read-only checks a normal browser would make (≤1–3 req/s):

1. Passive recon (P1): security headers, TLS/cert posture, cookie flags, HTTP→HTTPS
   redirect, `robots.txt` / `sitemap.xml` / `.well-known/*`, error-page/stack-trace
   leakage, technology + version fingerprinting.
2. Attack-surface map (P2): public pages, auth flows, API endpoints discovered from
   HTML/JS bundles, third-party integrations — inventory only.
3. Known-vuln lookup (P3) for any fingerprinted versions (OSV/NVD/GHSA/CISA KEV).
4. Check whether well-known sensitive paths exist (`.git`, `.env`, backups, admin
   panels, debug endpoints) with read-only GETs — report exposure, never exploit.

Do NOT send any crafted payload, auth attempt, IDOR/enumeration, or fuzzing — that is
active testing and requires the authorization gate (`$secaudit --active`). Clearly
state the passive-only coverage limits in the report.
